##### feat: write a per-run JSON record

The report prints and is gone. This rung adds `--record <path>`, a side channel that appends one
NDJSON object per bench result alongside the unchanged display. Design decisions taken at the
original pickup (2026-08-04):

- the record is per bench *result*, not per process: `all` emits one record per bench sharing
  the host / policy / clock stamp
- the display is never traded for the file: recording is a side channel, not a mode
- NDJSON, one object per line: `jq -s .` makes an array on demand, an interrupted run still
  parses, and per-run files concatenate with `cat`
- the tool names the file when handed a directory, because a fixed name is exactly what killed
  the powersave series (`run.sh` reused `u1.txt`..`p8.txt` and the rerun clobbered them)
  - `--record <dir>/` writes one file per run, stamped `<ts>-<host>-<bench>.ndjson`, and
    `--record <file>` appends to that file. The path's shape picks the mode
  - the open is `O_APPEND | O_CREAT`, never `O_TRUNC`, in both modes. The no-truncate invariant
    is what actually protects the evidence, whoever chose the name
  - basic ISO to the second in the filename (`20260804T093221Z`: no colons, lexicographic order
    is chronological order), RFC3339 with millis inside the record, plus the local offset as its
    own field. Millis are not decoration: `all` emits several records inside one second, so each
    also carries a process id and an index within the process
- `--tag k=v` is recorded verbatim and never interpreted, so a driving script labels condition /
  policy / box without the tool needing a notion of "series"
  - a per-run stamp is not a per-series stamp: only the caller knows which runs form one
    experiment, so `--tag series=<ts>` carries that, in every record of the series
  - no tag key is ever substituted into a path. That is where a template language starts
  - it lands with the record: a field of the same struct sharing all of its plumbing, so a rung
    of its own would review nothing
- the record carries a **fixed quantile ladder** (0.01 / 0.1 / 1 / 5 / 10 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 90 /
  95 / 99 / 99.9 / 99.99), not the report's populated bands, whose labels move with the data. It
  is what makes the A/B estimator question answerable after the fact, cheap now and impossible
  to backfill
- the record carries the **series of block means**, not just their summary: an aggregate cannot
  be decomposed, and the series is what lets within-run scatter be compared against across-run
  scatter. Bounded by a cap: keep every block mean while blocks <= 1000, summarize beyond
- the record documents its own fields, and a test enforces it
  - `describe-record`, a command word beside `all` / `qualify-environment`, prints the field
    dictionary: name, unit, one-line meaning. Not `--help`, which documents *inputs*
  - one source of truth is a const descriptor table, kept honest by a test that serializes a
    sample record, walks its keys, and fails on any key with no entry
  - every record carries `schema_version`, so a dictionary printed by today's binary can be
    checked against a record written by an older one
  - later polish, not this rung: per-field lookup (`explain frame_ns`) and generating README
    text from the same table
- absent is not zero: rpi5-20cd has no EPP and no `cpuinfo_avg_freq`, so every policy field is
  an `Option` recorded as absent
  - three states, not two: absent, present and uniform, present and split across policy groups.
    `freq::PolicyField` carries the token plus a `uniform` flag so the display can say
    `(mixed across CPUs)` rather than let one CPU stand in for the box
- ordering is part of the record: the 2026-08-03 pinned series was bimodal by *position*
  (p3-p6), which is invisible without a per-run wall-clock start
- comparison across the three boxes is within-box only: each box's pinned-vs-unpinned delta and
  its run-to-run scatter, never nanoseconds against nanoseconds

##### feat: qualify-environment reads the power policy

`qualify-environment` reads the policy as a fitness precondition and says so before spending
minutes on numbers it can predict will scatter. A diagnosis, never a mutation: setting the
governor needs root and is global and persistent, and the 2026-08-03 session's documented revert
left EPP at `performance` after the governor had already returned to `powersave`.

##### fix: LSC gains a run-to-run component

LSC is scoped to within-run block agreement but reads as a run-to-run bound. The best
configuration printed LSC 0.022 ns against a measured run-to-run stdev of 0.057 ns, so
single-run against single-run resolution is ~0.157 ns (0.71%) where the report prints 0.10%:
about 7x optimistic, and it did not improve when the environment did. Given the A/B purpose,
this is the cycle's most valuable rung.

- the fix is a **variance-versus-aggregation curve**, not a second measurement: a single run
  cannot measure run-to-run scatter directly. Aggregate its blocks in groups of 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
  and watch whether variance falls as `1/n`. Where it stops falling is the drift floor, and that
  floor is the run's honest resolution
  - this is Allan deviation (IEEE Std 1139), the standard tool in clock metrology for "how long
    should I average". The harness is already a clock project, so the machinery is familiar
  - the alternative, spawning children as `qualify-environment` does, is a much larger change
    and still cannot re-roll thermal or P-state history, so it does not reach the missing
    component
  - the duration estimate falls out of the same curve for free:
    `t_needed = t_now * (SE_now / SE_target)^2`, valid only where the `1/n` scaling still
    holds, which the curve is what tells us
- naming it accurately matters as much as computing it: a within-run bound must not print in a
  way that reads as a run-to-run one, which is the whole defect

##### feat: measure reproducibility closing

Closing out the cycle.

#### What the harness is for

**A/B comparison of algorithm changes**: did this change make it faster or slower. Stated here
because it decides calls like the rung specs above and is written down nowhere in the repo
(wink, 2026-08-04). It deserves a permanent home in the README's overview, and the cycle block
is where it landed first.

- the far tail is a validity check, not the score: beyond ~n4 on a 20 ns operation it measures
  OS interruptions (context switches, IRQs, faults, migrations), so it says whether to trust a
  comparison, never whether the algorithm improved
- the near tail is not in that bucket: cache miss rates, a ring's wrap boundary, and the 2t
  benches' producer/consumer phase relationships live around p99, and a change that improves the
  median while doubling p99 is usually a worse algorithm
- a comparison needs a resolution claim, not just a number, which is what makes the LSC rung
  load-bearing rather than last: an A/B verdict is only as good as the smallest delta the tool
  can honestly distinguish

#### The 2026-08-03 pinning experiment

The measurement that motivates the cycle (measured 2026-08-03, the session's terminal stamps
read 26-08-04 UTC):

- the measurement: `min-now --blocks 200`, 8 pinned + 8 unpinned per policy, alternating so box
  history is shared between conditions, under amd-pstate-epp `powersave` then `performance`
  - powersave unpinned: 23.927 ns, run-to-run stdev 0.785 ns (3.28%), grades 4 A / 2 D / 2 F
  - powersave pinned to one core: 22.207 ns, 0.073 ns (0.33%), all 8 graded D
  - performance unpinned: 21.980 ns, 0.057 ns (0.26%), no D or F in 17 runs
  - performance pinned: 22.359 ns, 0.311 ns (1.39%)
- what that supports, and how strongly:
  - the policy delta is big and one-directional: 8.9% on the unpinned mean, with unpinned
    run-to-run scatter falling from 0.785 ns to 0.057 ns
  - but policy could not be alternated the way pinning was (setting EPP needs root and is global
    and persistent), so the two policies are separated in time and the delta is confounded with
    box history. We think an effect this size survives de-confounding, but this experiment does
    not show it
  - pinning under powersave is the strongest result here: 7.2% off the mean and 10x off the
    scatter, on alternated runs
  - pinning under performance is the weakest: 1.7% *worse* than unpinned, and the whole gap is
    four consecutive pinned runs (p3-p6) at 22.59-22.70 ns while the pinned runs on either side
    sat at 22.08-22.09 ns and the interleaved unpinned runs did not move. So the 0.311 ns is the
    width of a state change, not scatter about a mean, and "pinning loses under performance"
    rests on that one cluster and should be treated as unreproduced
- the finding that reframes the grade: A was being awarded to the un-boosted floor. A powersave
  A run puts ~73% of its samples on 23.967 ns, the 3.7929 GHz TSC/base rate, while the boosted
  states are 21.79 / 22.22. Flatness is all the grade sees, and base clock is the flattest place
  on the box
- evidence is perishable: `tmp/pinexp/` held only the performance series (the rerun overwrote
  powersave), so the powersave numbers live only in the session transcript until copied into a
  chores design subsection
- cross-cuts the Todo entries below: the interpretation guide's worked trio and the blocks
  entry's duty-cycle evidence were both collected without recording the policy, and a four-run
  `--blocks` sweep proved confounded (block count and box history rose together, history
  dominating), so re-check those examples before they ship as teaching material
- raises "Seam-clock attribution": we think the three states map onto ~3.79 / 4.17 / 4.35 GHz,
  inferred from timing ratios alone, and a seam clock sample would settle it

#### The clock quantum and the dither

The clock's quantum is a property of the box, not the bench (measured on rpi5-20cd, 2026-08-04).
`inner` is sized for framing domination, `inner = ceil(10 * frame_ns / step_cost_ns)`, so in
`q = tick_ns / inner` the step cost cancels and `q / step = tick_ns / (10 * frame_ns)`.

- ~2.2% on the Pi (18.5185 ns tick, ~82 ns frame) against ~0.05% on the 3900X (0.264 ns tick,
  ~50 ns frame): a factor of 40, applying uniformly to every bench either box runs
- three benches confirm it, predicted `q` against the spacing between value clusters in the band
  table: `min-now` inner 23, q 0.805, seen 0.800 / 0.832 / 0.768. `zcr-with-1t` inner 47,
  q 0.394, seen 0.400 / 0.384 / 0.408. `zcr-with-2t` inner 4, q 4.630, seen 4.352 / 4.608 /
  4.864. The residual wobble is hdrhistogram bucketing (0.016 ns at 17 ns, 0.256 ns at 270 ns)
- so a printed per-sample spread below ~q describes the clock, not the workload: `min-now`'s
  `stdev p20..p80 0.403` is half a quantum and `zcr-with-1t`'s 0.213 is a two-point split, while
  `zcr-with-2t` spans ~11 quanta and its 4.906 is real to within 4% (`q/sqrt(12)` removed in
  quadrature)
- the means, the grades and LSC are unaffected: all work from batch or block means over ~1.2M
  samples, where quantization averages away as `1/sqrt(N)`
- so print and record it, do not size for it: `q` joined the `Setup:` block in the ported work,
  and `ticks_per_ns` and `inner` are record fields so it stays derivable per result
- a granularity floor on `inner` is the wrong fix and is its own Todo entry, not a rung here.
  The dither makes quantization zero-mean, so a 5M-sample mean carries `q/sqrt(12N)` = 0.0001 ns
  of it, while raising `inner` would smear the tail linearly and cannot reveal per-call shape
  below one tick either way
- the dither works on the coarse lattice, twice confirmed on the Pi: `zcr-with-1t`'s mass sits
  on two adjacent lattice points (2.08M at ~16.951, 2.94M at ~17.335) and interpolates to 17.18
  against a printed `mean z4..n2 17.183`, with the two-point stdev prediction 0.19 against a
  printed 0.213
  - so an off-lattice value is recovered rather than snapped, which is what `DITHER_SPAN` exists
    to do. The earlier worry that ~26-32 ns of span against an 18.5 ns quantum would bias it is
    not visible in the data
  - the decisive check remains cheap and unrun: sweep `-i` (23 / 97 / 233) on the Pi and confirm
    the mean does not move as `q` shrinks

+  A run puts ~73% of its samples on 23.967 ns, the 3.7929 GHz TSC/base rate, while the boosted
+  states are 21.79 / 22.22. Flatness is all the grade sees, and base clock is the flattest place
+  on the box

+  powersave), so the powersave numbers live only in the session transcript until copied into a
+  chores design subsection

+  entry's duty-cycle evidence were both collected without recording the policy, and a four-run
+  `--blocks` sweep proved confounded (block count and box history rose together, history
+  dominating), so re-check those examples before they ship as teaching material
+- raises "Seam-clock attribution": we think the three states map onto ~3.79 / 4.17 / 4.35 GHz,
+  inferred from timing ratios alone, and a seam clock sample would settle it
+#### The clock quantum and the dither
+The clock's quantum is a property of the box, not the bench (measured on rpi5-20cd, 2026-08-04).
+`inner` is sized for framing domination, `inner = ceil(10 * frame_ns / step_cost_ns)`, so in
+`q = tick_ns / inner` the step cost cancels and `q / step = tick_ns / (10 * frame_ns)`.
+- ~2.2% on the Pi (18.5185 ns tick, ~82 ns frame) against ~0.05% on the 3900X (0.264 ns tick,

+- three benches confirm it, predicted `q` against the spacing between value clusters in the band

+  `zcr-with-2t` spans ~11 quanta and its 4.906 is real to within 4% (`q/sqrt(12)` removed in
+  quadrature)
+- the means, the grades and LSC are unaffected: all work from batch or block means over ~1.2M
+  samples, where quantization averages away as `1/sqrt(N)`
+- so print and record it, do not size for it: `q` joined the `Setup:` block in the ported work,
+  and `ticks_per_ns` and `inner` are record fields so it stays derivable per result
+- a granularity floor on `inner` is the wrong fix and is its own Todo entry, not a rung here.

may or many not know how and when that actually happens. I've been programming for more than 50y
and I'm no expert in this area. Also, no need to say more than this is a continuation of a
previous thread.

One other thing we have a `qualify-environment` that spits out some numbers and I was exploring
how well it's working at the moment. What I learned it currently states 3900x is lousy and 7600x
works pretty well. ATM I can't speak to the accuracy or precision of the result from based on

Your thoughts only on my thoughts.

content.text:
Thoughts on both:

**Your power-policy model is right, and it's the right level for the Problem statement.** Two refinements worth building into the wording:

- The policy doesn't pick a frequency, it picks *eagerness*. Concretely it's the kernel's cpufreq governor plus, on modern AMD, the EPP hint (`amd-pstate-epp powersave`/`performance`): a knob that decides how quickly the chip boosts under load and how quickly it retreats to save power. So "power saving mode" isn't a mode the box sits in — it's a per-moment decision driven by recent load history, which is why it bites benchmarks on idle desktops and servers, not just laptops on battery.
- For measurement, the enemy isn't low frequency, it's *moving* frequency. A ~20 ns operation is cycles × cycle time, so the number tracks the clock directly. Our 2026-08-03 data made both failure shapes concrete: under powersave the same code differed by ~9% run to run with the clock wandering between states, and — the sneaky one — a "clean-looking" powersave run was flat because it sat on the un-boosted base clock the whole time. Flat and slow grades as beautifully as flat and fast. Your "highest sustainable frequency, consistently" is the practical goal; the precise need is "a known, stable clock state" — and since setting the policy needs root and is global, the harness's job is to *record and report* it, never to change it. That's the actual problem sentence: today's reports don't record the policy, so a reader can't tell a code delta from a power-management delta.

Agreed also on trimming the history: one sentence ("continues the cycle stalled since 2026-08-04") and the port mechanics stay in Deliberation where they already live.

**On qualify-environment**: your read matches the independent evidence — the 7600x's five identical A/0.81s/16.2 ns rows are about as clean as the tool could show, and the 3900x is the same box where the bistable-state behavior was measured directly. But one output is already self-contradicting: the 3900x's 0.01s "settle" next to F grades claims the box was steady from the start *and* that a transition landed mid-window. We think the settle detector is being fooled by the same thing that fooled the grade — base clock is the flattest place on the box, so a run that starts on the un-boosted floor looks "settled" immediately. And your calibration method (does the verdict fit experience?) is currently the only one available — which is precisely what this cycle improves: once runs write records with the policy and the block-mean series, the tool's claims can be scored against measured run-to-run scatter instead of judgment, and the policy rung will let it say *why* the 3900x scatters (powersave) instead of just stamping F.

The plain version: your picture is correct — the chip speeds up and slows down on its own to save power, and our numbers move with it. The fix this cycle promises is not to control that, but to always write down what the power settings were, so when two runs disagree you can tell whether the code changed or the computer did. And the suspicious "settles in 0.01s" on the 3900x is probably the tool mistaking "stuck at slow speed" for "warmed up and steady."

Want me to rewrite the Problem statement along these lines?

message.content: For comparision purposes that we don't need to run fast we need to run consistently. A stable frequency at any rate is better than every unstable frequency. Is there a way we can ask the OS to "pin" the frequency? Can we produce a quality number on the stability of the frequency?

content.text:
Both answers are yes, with useful nuance:

**Pinning the frequency.** Linux gives three knobs, in increasing order of force:

- **Governor/EPP** (what we have now): `performance` doesn't pin, it just boosts eagerly — the clock still moves.
- **Clamp the range**: set `scaling_min_freq` equal to `scaling_max_freq` (per CPU in `/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/`, or `cpupower frequency-set -d X -u X`). With `amd-pstate` this writes the hardware's min/max perf limits, so the chip's own boost logic is boxed into one state.
- **Boost off**: `echo 0 > /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/boost`. Pinning *at or below base clock with boost off* is the stable configuration — the firmware's opportunistic 25 MHz-step boosting (which is what makes the 3900x wander) has nowhere to go, and thermal throttling is unlikely to reach down that far.

Your principle is exactly why pin-below-base is acceptable: we lose maybe 15% speed and gain a clock that holds one value for the whole run and the same value next week. Caveats: all of it needs root, is global, and persists — so per the "diagnosis, never mutation" rule already in the ladder, the harness should never do this itself. The right shape is a documented recipe (README or a `setup-pinned-clock.sh` the *user* runs) plus the record rung capturing governor, EPP, min/max, and boost — then a pinned run is verifiable from its record, not from trust. Two honest limits: a cpufreq pin bounds the *requested* state, not physics (thermal limits can still dip below it, rare below base), and clock stability isn't the only wobble source — idle-state wake latency is a separate knob — but it's the dominant one our data shows.

**A stability quality number.** Two complementary layers, both already latent in the plan:

- **Direct**: sample the clock at batch seams — the reader exists (`src/freq.rs`), and "Seam-clock attribution" is already a Todo. From the seam series you get a real metric: median frequency, spread, and count of distinct states/transitions. Something like "clock: 4.35 GHz, held within 1% for 98% of seams, 0 transitions" is a quality number a programmer can read, and it would let `qualify-environment` say *why* a run scattered instead of stamping F. It would also catch the 0.01s-settle lie directly: a run sitting on base clock would show as "stable at 3.79 GHz", visibly different from "stable at 4.35 GHz".
- **Indirect, and already a rung**: the LSC rung's variance-versus-aggregation curve is the metrology-grade stability number for the thing we ultimately care about — measured time per operation. The frequency samples are the *attribution* (was the clock the cause), the drift floor is the *consequence* (how much resolution it cost). Together they answer both "is the box stable" and "stable enough for what".

The natural question is whether seam-clock sampling should be promoted from the Todo list into this cycle — it's the piece that turns the stability number from inference into measurement, and the record rung is where its samples would want to be written anyway. I'd hold that decision until the record rung is being laddered in detail, and I've said nothing in the block about it yet — your call when you're ready.

The plain version: yes, the OS can hold the clock at one speed — set the minimum and maximum to the same value and turn boost off, which needs admin rights, so it's a setup step a person does, and our tool's job is to write down that it was done. And yes, we can score stability: sample the actual clock during the run and report how much it moved, alongside the existing statistics that show what the movement cost.

(the cpufreq governor plus, on AMD, the EPP hint) decides how eagerly the chip boosts under load

unstable fast one. Today the harness cannot report the policy, cannot hold the clock still, and

Done. The block now reflects the new scope:

- **Problem** rewritten for a typical programmer: CPUs continuously change clock frequency to save power, the OS's power policy (governor + EPP hint) decides how eagerly they boost and retreat, a latency number is cycles times cycle time, and the 2026-08-03 evidence shows both failure shapes (~9% run-to-run wander under powersave, and the flat-but-slow base-clock run grading A). Your principle is in it verbatim as the requirement: consistency, not speed — a stable clock at any rate beats an unstable fast one. The history is now one parenthetical: "(Continues the cycle stalled since 2026-08-04.)"
- **New rung**: `feat: read, pin, and restore the CPU frequency`, between the record rung and the policy rung. Its spec carries your design: the three command words, `read-freq` rootless and shaped for a prompt or status bar, pin = min=max + boost off at or below base, pin-at-start/restore-at-exit catching normal return, panic, and SIGINT/SIGTERM, and — since "always" is best-effort against SIGKILL — `pin-freq` saves the displaced state to a file *before* touching anything, so `restore-freq` recovers even after an unclean death.
- **Acceptance check** gained a measure: pin-then-restore leaves the box exactly as found, and the crash-recovery path works.
- **Deliberation** records the reversal explicitly: the old diagnosis-never-mutation rule's reasons (root, global, persistent) become design constraints instead — explicit opt-in, state saved first, every catchable path restores. `qualify-environment` itself stays read-only; the mutation lives only in the commands.
- The record rung's spec now names the clamp and boost state as record fields, so a pinned run is verifiable from its record, and the three-box rerun note moved to sit after the frequency rung so the rerun can add a pinned-clock condition.

One design point worth your eye when you review: I specified that `pin-freq` over an existing save refuses to overwrite it (so a double-pin can't destroy the true pre-pin state) — the alternative is last-write-wins, which is simpler but loses the original state exactly when someone is fumbling. Everything else is as you described.

The spec now carries the declarative-restore design throughout:

- **`restore-freq` converges to the user's declared steady state** — declared once in the existing layered config (a `[freq]` section, normally the XDG file `~/.config/iiac-perf/config.toml`, since the steady state belongs to the box, not the project). No transient state file exists at all.
- The rejection rationale is recorded in both the rung spec and Deliberation: the save-and-restore-what-we-found draft is named and rejected on your two grounds — transient files are a demonstrated failure mode in this repo, and displaced-state restore ratchets on back-to-back runs (run 2 "restores" run 1's pin), worst on a laptop or phone. Convergence is idempotent from any starting point, so the uncatchable exit paths (SIGKILL, power loss) need no recovery state — `restore-freq` works from anywhere, any time.
- The no-declaration case: `pin-freq` refuses until a steady state is declared (no pinning with no way home), and `read-freq` can print the current state in config form ready to paste — which also gives you the one-command setup path.
- The acceptance check now tests the right contract: pin-then-restore lands the box in the *declared* state, and restore converges after an unclean death.
- The qualify-environment spec's cross-reference updated to match: the 2026-08-03 bad-revert story now motivates "declared, not remembered" rather than the state file.

One note on naming: you wrote `.vc-config.md` — I took the intent as "a persistent per-box config" and homed it in iiac-perf's own existing config layering rather than the vc-x1 dual-repo config, which belongs to the repo tooling, not the harness. If you actually meant a separate standalone file, say so and I'll adjust the spec.

1	# vc-config: settable configuration keys
2	
3	This file is two things at once, and that is the point: the **schema prototype** vc-x1 is built
4	from, and the **long-form documentation** every generated `reference:` url lands on. One `##`
5	section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence, that key's metadata, so
6	the documentation and the schema cannot describe different keys.
7	
8	It is not a config file. Your workspace's config is `.vc-config.md` (note the leading dot).
9	Editing this file changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build, and is reviewed
10	like any source change.
11	
12	## How this file is read
13	
14	The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
15	order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
16	instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
17	outside the fences never reaches a parser.
18	
19	Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
20	(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
21	entries a key's table may carry:
22	
23	- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
24	  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
25	  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
26	    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
27	  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-bot"`: the work side's and the bot side's instance config
28	- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"item-list"`
29	- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
30	- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
31	  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
32	- `default`: the built-in value; omit when there is none
33	- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
34	- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs; the value is role-specific, filled by
35	  `init`
36	- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs; when absent (the norm) build.rs derives
37	  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
38	  below
39	
40	## The prototype's own metadata
41	
42	`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
43	repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
44	and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
45	is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.
46	
47	```toml
48	[vc-config]
49	reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
50	```
51	
52	## How the keys resolve
53	
54	The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
55	instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.
56	The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in the user
57	config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.
58	
59	## default.account
60	
61	The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
62	the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.
63	
64	```toml
65	[default.account]
66	homes = ["user"]
67	kind = "str"
68	doc = "Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use when --account is absent"
69	used-by = "--account (init and account-aware commands)"
70	example = "work"
71	```
72	
73	## default.debug
74	
75	Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
76	yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.
77	
78	```toml
79	[default.debug]
80	homes = ["user"]
81	kind = "str"
82	doc = "Default --debug value when used without an argument (reserved; not yet consumed)"
83	used-by = "--debug (reserved; not yet consumed)"
84	example = "true"
85	```
86	
87	## repo.default
88	
89	The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
90	[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
91	your own.
92	
93	```toml
94	[repo.default]
95	homes = ["user"]
96	kind = "str"
97	doc = "Default repo category when --repo is bare: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
98	used-by = "--repo (default category when --repo is bare)"
99	example = "acmehousing"
100	```
101	
102	## repo.category.\<cat\>
103	
104	The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
105	`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
106	when its target is a path or a bare name.
107	
108	```toml
109	[repo.category."<cat>"]
110	homes = ["user"]
111	kind = "str"
112	doc = "Literal value for repo category <cat>: a remote URL prefix (init appends /<NAME>.git) or a local parent dir"
113	used-by = "--repo <cat> (init remote/local resolution)"
114	example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
115	```
116	
117	## account.\<name\>.repo.default
118	
119	Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
120	`<name>` account profile is active.
121	
122	```toml
123	[account."<name>".repo.default]
124	homes = ["user"]
125	kind = "str"
126	doc = "Per-account default repo category: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
127	used-by = "--account <name> with --repo"
128	example = "acmehousing"
129	```
130	
131	## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>
132	
133	Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
134	account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.
135	
136	```toml
137	[account."<name>".repo.category."<cat>"]
138	homes = ["user"]
139	kind = "str"
140	doc = "Per-account literal value for repo category <cat> (remote URL prefix or local parent dir)"
141	used-by = "--account <name> with --repo <cat>"
142	example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
143	```
144	
145	## bot-session.items
146	
147	The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
148	`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
149	individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.
150	
151	```toml
152	[bot-session.items]
153	homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
154	kind = "item-list"
155	doc = "Default bot-session item set (comma-separated)"
156	used-by = "bot-session --<item> / --no-<item> / --all / --none"
157	default = "headers,user,assistant,tool,summary"
158	```
159	
160	## bot-session.result-lines
161	
162	Maximum lines shown per tool result in the conversation view when results are rendered; `0`
163	means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.
164	
165	```toml
166	[bot-session.result-lines]
167	homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
168	kind = "usize"
169	doc = "Default --result-lines: max lines shown per tool result (0 = unlimited)"
170	used-by = "bot-session --result-lines"
171	default = 10
172	```
173	
174	## bot-session.col-width
175	
176	First-column width in `bot-session`'s field-inventory views: `--fields`, `--unknown`, and
177	`--per-line`. The conversation view never consults it. The built-in default aligns the type
178	column for ~99% of observed key paths: every structural key except a long tail of
179	`snapshot.trackedFileBackups.<absolute path>.*` keys, whose embedded absolute paths can be
180	arbitrarily long and so are left to overflow. The `--col-width` flag overrides it.
181	
182	```toml
183	[bot-session.col-width]
184	homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
185	kind = "usize"
186	doc = "Default --col-width: first-column width in the --fields / --unknown / --per-line views"
187	used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
188	default = 68
189	```
190	
191	## repos.work
192	
193	The work repo's path, relative to the config file's directory: `"."` in the work repo, `".."`
194	in the bot repo. Structural: written by `init`, read by workspace-root discovery, and the entry
195	that resolves to the config's own directory names that file's side. Every instance config must
196	carry it.
197	
198	```toml
199	[repos.work]
200	homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
201	kind = "str"
202	doc = "The work repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (\".\" in the work repo, \"..\" in the bot repo); the entry resolving to the config's own directory names the side"
203	used-by = "find_workspace_root, side detection (structural; written by init)"
204	required = true
205	example = "."
206	```
207	
208	## repos.bot
209

# vc-config: settable configuration keys

This file is two things at once, and that is the point: the **schema prototype** vc-x1 is built
from, and the **long-form documentation** every generated `reference:` url lands on. One `##`
section per settable key holds that key's prose and, in a `toml` fence, that key's metadata, so
the documentation and the schema cannot describe different keys.

It is not a config file. Your workspace's config is `.vc-config.md` (note the leading dot).
Editing this file changes what the binary knows, takes effect on the next build, and is reviewed
like any source change.

## How this file is read

The format is the config markdown carrier's own: the `toml` fences, concatenated in document
order, form the TOML that gets parsed. build.rs shares the filter (`src/md_fence.rs`) with the
instance-config loader, so the prototype and a `.vc-config.md` are read by one rule, and prose
outside the fences never reaches a parser.

Shape: one TOML table per settable key, named by the key's path, dynamic segments quoted
(`[repo.category."<cat>"]`). Key order here is rendering order everywhere downstream. The
entries a key's table may carry:

- `homes`: which config file(s) may contain the key. vc-x1 writes it only into those files, and
  `vc-x1 config --validate` reports it as unknown anywhere else. The values:
  - `"user"`: the user-wide config, `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` (or
    `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vc-x1/config.toml`). One per user, still TOML rather than markdown
  - `"workspace-code"`, `"workspace-bot"`: the work side's and the bot side's instance config
- `kind`: value shape, one of `"str"`, `"usize"`, `"item-list"`
- `doc`: one-line description (rendered into generated configs, so keep it tight)
- `used-by`: what reads the value once it is set, which is a different question from `homes`:
  the command or flag it feeds, or the structural role it plays
- `default`: the built-in value; omit when there is none
- `example`: representative value for keys with no default
- `required`: active (not commented) in generated configs; the value is role-specific, filled by
  `init`
- `reference`: optional override url for the key's docs; when absent (the norm) build.rs derives
  `<reference-base>/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#<anchor of the path>`, which is the key's own section
  below

## The prototype's own metadata

`[vc-config]` is this file's metadata rather than a settable key. `reference-base` is the bare
repo url every derived reference is built from: build.rs joins it with `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md#`
and the key's heading anchor, so a reference follows the repo's default branch and no branch name
is baked in. A fork points it at its own repo and edits its own copy of this file.

```toml
[vc-config]
reference-base = "https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1"
```

## How the keys resolve

The `bot-session.*` keys resolve git-style, most specific wins: CLI flag, then the workspace
instance config, then the user config (`~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml`), then the built-in default.
The other keys live in a single home each: `default.*`, `repo.*`, and `account.*` in the user
config, `repos.*` in the workspace configs.

## default.account

The account profile `init` and other account-aware commands use when `--account` is not given on
the command line: the name of an `[account.<name>]` section in the user config.

```toml
[default.account]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Account profile (an [account.<name>] section) to use when --account is absent"
used-by = "--account (init and account-aware commands)"
example = "work"
```

## default.debug

Reserved: the value `--debug` would assume when used without an argument. No command consumes it
yet; setting it is harmless and does nothing.

```toml
[default.debug]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default --debug value when used without an argument (reserved; not yet consumed)"
used-by = "--debug (reserved; not yet consumed)"
example = "true"
```

## repo.default

The repo category `--repo` assumes when given bare (no `<cat>` argument): the name of a
[repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat) entry, one of the built-ins (`remote`, `local`) or
your own.

```toml
[repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Default repo category when --repo is bare: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--repo (default category when --repo is bare)"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## repo.category.\<cat\>

The literal value behind a repo category name: a remote url prefix (`init` appends
`/<NAME>.git`) or a local parent directory. `init` resolves `--repo <cat>` through this table
when its target is a path or a bare name.

```toml
[repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Literal value for repo category <cat>: a remote URL prefix (init appends /<NAME>.git) or a local parent dir"
used-by = "--repo <cat> (init remote/local resolution)"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.default

Per-account variant of [repo.default](#repodefault): the default category used while the
`<name>` account profile is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.default]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account default repo category: a [repo.category.<cat>] name: a built-in (remote, local) or your own"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo"
example = "acmehousing"
```

## account.\<name\>.repo.category.\<cat\>

Per-account variant of [repo.category.\<cat\>](#repocategorycat): a category defined inside an
account profile, shadowing the top-level table while that account is active.

```toml
[account."<name>".repo.category."<cat>"]
homes = ["user"]
kind = "str"
doc = "Per-account literal value for repo category <cat> (remote URL prefix or local parent dir)"
used-by = "--account <name> with --repo <cat>"
example = "git@github.com:acmehousing"
```

## bot-session.items

The default item set the `bot-session` conversation view renders, a comma-separated list (e.g.
`headers,user,assistant,tool,summary`). The per-item `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` flags override
individual items, and `--all` / `--none` replace the base set entirely.

```toml
[bot-session.items]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "item-list"
doc = "Default bot-session item set (comma-separated)"
used-by = "bot-session --<item> / --no-<item> / --all / --none"
default = "headers,user,assistant,tool,summary"
```

## bot-session.result-lines

Maximum lines shown per tool result in the conversation view when results are rendered; `0`
means unlimited. The `--result-lines` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.result-lines]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --result-lines: max lines shown per tool result (0 = unlimited)"
used-by = "bot-session --result-lines"
default = 10
```

## bot-session.col-width

First-column width in `bot-session`'s field-inventory views: `--fields`, `--unknown`, and
`--per-line`. The conversation view never consults it. The built-in default aligns the type
column for ~99% of observed key paths: every structural key except a long tail of
`snapshot.trackedFileBackups.<absolute path>.*` keys, whose embedded absolute paths can be
arbitrarily long and so are left to overflow. The `--col-width` flag overrides it.

```toml
[bot-session.col-width]
homes = ["user", "workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "usize"
doc = "Default --col-width: first-column width in the --fields / --unknown / --per-line views"
used-by = "bot-session --col-width"
default = 68
```

## repos.work

The work repo's path, relative to the config file's directory: `"."` in the work repo, `".."`
in the bot repo. Structural: written by `init`, read by workspace-root discovery, and the entry
that resolves to the config's own directory names that file's side. Every instance config must
carry it.

```toml
[repos.work]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The work repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (\".\" in the work repo, \"..\" in the bot repo); the entry resolving to the config's own directory names the side"
used-by = "find_workspace_root, side detection (structural; written by init)"
required = true
example = "."
```

## repos.bot

The bot repo's path, relative to the config file's directory (e.g. `".claude"` in the work
repo, `"."` in the bot repo). Its presence is what signals dual-repo mode; a single-repo
workspace simply omits it.

```toml
[repos.bot]
homes = ["workspace-code", "workspace-bot"]
kind = "str"
doc = "The bot repo's path, relative to this config file's directory (e.g. \".claude\" in the work repo, \".\" in the bot repo); presence signals dual-repo mode"
used-by = "default_scope, scope resolution, ochid prefixes (structural)"
example = ".claude"
```

input.description: Read the settle function's rule

content.text:
Having read the actual mechanism, here's my rating — and the 0.01s is now fully explained, not just suspected:

**The verdict layer: good, and honestly built.** The grades read the right signals (the drift/step transition detectors over the bench phase are what caught the 3900x's wandering), the "box is the subject" framing is correct, and both boxes' verdicts are corroborated by independent evidence — the 3900x is the same machine where the bistable states were measured directly, and the 7600x's five identical rows are as clean as the tool could show. Crucially, the settle cell is *read but not scored* — there's a test pinning that (`settle_cell_is_read_but_not_scored`) — so the broken number never contaminates the verdict. That's why your expectations and the grades agree while settle is nonsense: the defect is quarantined by design.

**The settle cell: broken for exactly the case this cycle targets, and the code already half-knows it.** `gauge::settle` reports the earliest suffix of the *warmup* stretch that grades A on *timing alone*. Two consequences on the 3900x under powersave:

- A box sitting flat on one P-state grades A immediately — flat is all the grade sees — so settle reads 0.01s. "Settled" here means "stopped moving," not "reached the operating state it will hold through measurement." It then transitions mid-bench and the bench grades F. Both cells are truthful about what they measure; together they mislead.
- The fix already exists one function away: the warmup *exit* classifier (`classify_warm`) gates timing-A behind `clock_stable` — its own doc comment says "steady is not settled when the box is mid-climb (the measured 7600x dwell)". But `settle()` was never given the clock series, so the settle cell still believes timing alone. The design learned the lesson at the exit and didn't propagate it to the display.

**Accuracy: unquantified, as you said yourself.** Right now the tool is calibrated only against your expectations — which it passes — but nothing scores its claims against measured run-to-run scatter. That's precisely what this cycle's rungs change: the record rung makes its inputs durable (and would let it read records instead of the brittle-but-loud text parsing it does today), the policy rung lets it say *why* a box scatters instead of stamping F, and the frequency work gives settle the vocabulary it's missing — "settled at 3.79 GHz base clock" is diagnostic where "0.01s" is a lie of omission.

Overall: I'd rate the verdict machinery a solid B+ — right answers, right structure, honest quarantine of the weak cell — and the settle cell a D, wrong in exactly the powersave case that matters most. The cheapest worthwhile fix is passing the clock series into `settle()` with the same gate the exit already uses, plus naming the state it settled into. That reads like a bullet on the qualify-environment rung's spec — say the word and I'll add it.

The plain version: the pass/fail judgment is trustworthy and your instinct about it matches how it's built — the suspicious "settles in 0.01 seconds" is kept out of the scoring on purpose. That number is wrong because "settled" currently means "the timing went flat," and a computer stuck at its slow speed is perfectly flat. The machinery to check the actual clock speed already exists in the warmup code; the settle display just doesn't use it yet, and this cycle's planned work is what fixes that properly.

content.text:
Right now it's a bullet on the qualify-environment rung — and having thought about your question, that's the wrong home. Here's the how, and where I'd move it:

**How.** The mechanics are already in place, which is what makes this cheap: warmup already collects a clock series alongside the probe series, and `classify_warm` (src/harness.rs:880) already gates its timing-A verdict behind `clock_stable`. The fix is to hand that same clock series to `gauge::settle` so a warmup suffix only counts as settled when the clock also held still across it, and to extend the cell to name the state — `0.81s @ 4.35 GHz` (or "settled at base clock") instead of a bare time. One ripple: `qualify-environment`'s `parse_settle` reads the cell text, so the parser updates with the format. `Settle::Never` and the read-but-not-scored quarantine stay as they are.

**What rung.** It deserves to be its own small rung — `fix: the settle cell reads the clock` — placed as the first Work rung, right after the opening, ahead of the record rung. Three reasons:

- **No dependencies.** It needs nothing from the config, frequency, or policy rungs — the clock series exists today. It's ready now.
- **Diffs should read as their titles.** The change lands in `gauge.rs`/`harness.rs` and improves every report's grade block. Buried in the qualify rung, that rung's diff would say "policy precondition" while half of it edits the gauge.
- **Order protects the evidence.** Landing it before the record rung means no archived record ever carries the misleading 0.01s, and landing before the three-box rerun means the rerun's settle cells are honest — the rerun is exactly where a lying settle would get quoted for years.

The ladder would become: opening → **fix: the settle cell reads the clock** → JSON record → markdown config carrier → freq commands → (rerun) → qualify reads policy → LSC → closing. The qualify rung keeps a one-line pointer (it inherits the corrected cell and its parser update), and the spec bullet I added moves to the new rung's `Ladder details`.

message.content: In the config file how are the range of valid values for "freq" determined? Can the app determine a suggested "best" value fort testing? For instance running many short duration with X length gaps might be better/worse then fewer longer duration runs with some Y length gaps.

content.text:
Good questions — the first has a clean sysfs answer, the second is genuinely a measurement question, and your X/Y scheduling instinct is the reason there's no schedule-free "best".

**How the valid range is determined.** The box publishes it, per policy group, in the same sysfs directory the pin writes to: `cpuinfo_min_freq` / `cpuinfo_max_freq` are the hardware limits, `scaling_min_freq` / `scaling_max_freq` the current clamp. On modern drivers (amd-pstate, the 3900x/7600x) the range is effectively continuous between those bounds; on older or embedded drivers (the Pi's cpufreq-dt, acpi-cpufreq) there's a discrete menu in `scaling_available_frequencies`, and a pin must pick from it. Two consequences for our design: the config can't be validated in the abstract, only against the box — right timing is at `pin-freq` time, with an error that prints the valid range read from sysfs (and `read-freq` should print that range too, so the user picks informed). And heterogeneous boxes (phone big.LITTLE) have different ranges per policy group, which is why the spec already reads state "per policy group".

**Can the app suggest a best value?** Yes, empirically — and only empirically, because "best" means "highest frequency the box *holds* under this workload", and that's thermal, not tabular. The shape is a calibration search: start from max-with-boost-off, pin, drive a bench-like load, and verify with machinery we already have (`clock_stable` plus the grade); step down until a candidate holds clean, report it. The safe no-search default remains base clock — guaranteed sustainable by definition, which is why the spec recommends at-or-below-base.

**Your X/Y point is the catch, and it's real.** Whether a frequency is sustainable depends on the duty cycle: our own 2026-08-02 data showed sustained load climbing into the fast state while 5 ms bursts between sleeps held the slow one, and thermal limits work the other way (a short run passes at a frequency a long run throttles from). So a suggested pin is only valid *for a schedule*: a `suggest-freq` would need to dwell at least as long as the runs you intend, and its honest output is "stable at F for runs of duration D with gap G", not a bare number. The pleasant part: deciding many-short-vs-few-long is exactly what this cycle's machinery answers — the record rung's block-mean series plus the LSC rung's variance-versus-aggregation curve tell you where averaging stops helping within a run (favoring more, shorter runs beyond that), and `--tag`-labeled record series let you measure the X/Y tradeoff directly instead of guessing.

My recommendation: fold the *validation* half (range read from sysfs, checked at pin time, printed by `read-freq`) into the freq rung's spec now — it's load-bearing for the commands. Leave `suggest-freq` out of this cycle's ladder: it wants the record and LSC rungs landed first, since they supply the evidence a suggestion is judged by, so it's a natural follow-up Todo entry instead. Want me to make those two edits?

The plain version: the computer itself publishes the legal speed range, so the tool checks your chosen value against the machine when it pins, not before. The tool could also hunt for the best speed by trying values and watching whether the machine holds them, but the answer depends on how you run your tests — long runs heat the chip more than short bursts — so any suggestion has to name the test pattern it was measured under. The safe default stays "base clock": the speed the chip can always hold.

39	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
40	in scope:
41	
42	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
43	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
comment text it doesn't reflow.

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected, while inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.

1	//! The `qualify-environment` selftest: is this machine fit to
2	//! measure on?
3	//!
4	//! Respawns our own binary `--runs` times at `--gap`, collects
5	//! each run's environment grade, prints the table, and returns a
6	//! verdict. It tests the *machine*, not a workload, so it reads
7	//! the environment stretches rather than the run grade — see
8	//! [`crate::gauge::EnvGrade`].
9	//!
10	//! - **Why respawn** rather than loop in-process: a fresh process
11	//!   per run is what terminal use looks like, and in-process
12	//!   repeats would share warmed state — the very thing under
13	//!   test.
14	//! - **Why `min-now`** as the child workload: the box is the
15	//!   subject, so the leanest available bench is right. It also
16	//!   measures nearly what the probe measures, which keeps the run
17	//!   grade and the environment grade commensurable.
18	//! - **The verdict** is grades, not values: median environment
19	//!   grade at B or better, and no run whose `drift` or `step`
20	//!   reached D/F in either stretch. Those two are the transition
21	//!   detectors, so a D/F there is a state change landing inside a
22	//!   measurement window — the anomaly this test exists to catch.
23	//!   Wobble on `spread` or `interference` is ambient
24	//!   contamination and does not fail the run.
25	
26	use std::process::Command;
27	use std::time::Duration;
28	
29	use crate::gauge::Settle;
30	
31	/// Child bench: the leanest registered workload, so the table
32	/// reflects the box rather than a workload's character.
33	const CHILD_BENCH: &str = "min-now";
34	
35	/// Knobs for one selftest, from the CLI.
36	pub struct QualifyCfg {
37	    /// Child runs to spawn.
38	    pub runs: u64,
39	    /// Sleep before each child. Zero sustains the duty cycle that
40	    /// provokes a transition; a nonzero gap probes a quieter one.
41	    pub gap_s: f64,
42	    /// Wall-clock seconds per child run.
43	    pub duration_s: f64,
44	    /// `--pin` spec to pass through, if any.
45	    pub pin: Option<String>,
46	    /// Print the table and skip the verdict.
47	    pub print_only: bool,
48	    /// `--settle-time` to pass each child, when the parent was
49	    /// given one. Absent leaves each child on its own default, so
50	    /// the table reflects what a plain run of this binary does.
51	    pub settle_time: Option<f64>,
52	}
53	
54	/// One environment stretch parsed from a child's grade-block
55	/// row: its composite (`worst` column) and the two transition
56	/// detectors' letters.
57	struct Stretch {
58	    letter: char,
59	    drift: Option<char>,
60	    step: Option<char>,
61	}
62	
63	/// Split one report line into grade-block cells: columns are
64	/// right-aligned with a two-space minimum gap, so two-or-more
65	/// spaces is the cell separator and single spaces stay inside a
66	/// cell (`0.30% A`, `not settled`, `9.37% @1.90s D`).
67	fn row_cells(line: &str) -> Vec<&str> {
68	    line.split("  ")
69	        .map(str::trim)
70	        .filter(|s| !s.is_empty())
71	        .collect()
72	}
73	
74	/// A cell's trailing grade letter, `None` for a blank cell or
75	/// anything else that does not end in A-F.
76	fn cell_letter(cell: &str) -> Option<char> {
77	    cell.chars().last().filter(|c| ('A'..='F').contains(c))
78	}
79	
80	/// A warmup row's `settle` cell: `0.84s @4.35GHz`, a bare
81	/// `0.84s` when the child's clock was unreadable, `not settled`,
82	/// or a blank when the child had nothing to report.
83	fn parse_settle(cell: &str) -> Option<Settle> {
84	    match cell {
85	        "not settled" => Some(Settle::Never),
86	        _ => {
87	            let mut tokens = cell.split_whitespace();
88	            let t_s = tokens.next()?.strip_suffix('s')?.parse().ok()?;
89	            let ghz = tokens
90	                .next()
91	                .and_then(|g| g.strip_prefix('@')?.strip_suffix("GHz")?.parse().ok());
92	            Some(Settle::At { t_s, ghz })
93	        }
94	    }
95	}
96	
97	/// Parse one grade-block row's cells into a [`Stretch`]. Cell
98	/// order is the block's column order: grade, phase, settle,
99	/// worst, spread, bursts, interference, drift, step.
100	fn parse_stretch(cells: &[&str]) -> Stretch {
101	    Stretch {
102	        letter: cells.get(3).and_then(|c| c.chars().next()).unwrap_or('?'), // OK: short row can't happen, '?' scores worst if it does
103	        drift: cells.get(7).copied().and_then(cell_letter),
104	        step: cells.get(8).copied().and_then(cell_letter),
105	    }
106	}
107	
108	impl Stretch {
109	    /// True when a transition detector reached D/F here.
110	    fn transition_degraded(&self) -> bool {
111	        [self.drift, self.step]
112	            .into_iter()
113	            .flatten()
114	            .any(|l| l == 'D' || l == 'F')
115	    }
116	}
117	
118	/// One child run's parsed result.
119	struct QualifyRun {
120	    warmup: Option<Stretch>,
121	    during: Option<Stretch>,
122	    /// Environment composite — the worse of the two stretches,
123	    /// computed here from their `worst` columns.
124	    worst: char,
125	    /// The run's mean, for the value column: the number that makes
126	    /// a two-state box visible at a glance.
127	    mean: String,
128	    /// How long the child's warmup took to settle: how much
129	    /// warming this box needs before it is worth measuring on,
130	    /// read across respawns. Reported, not judged: the verdict
131	    /// stays grades, because a box still moving at the end of
132	    /// warmup already shows up as a drift/step D/F on the warmup
133	    /// stretch.
134	    settle: Option<Settle>,
135	}
136	
137	impl QualifyRun {
138	    /// True when either stretch shows a transition at D/F.
139	    fn transition_degraded(&self) -> bool {
140	        [self.warmup.as_ref(), self.during.as_ref()]
141	            .into_iter()
142	            .flatten()
143	            .any(Stretch::transition_degraded)
144	    }
145	
146	    /// Per-stretch letters for the table, `-` where a stretch is
147	    /// absent (`--no-env-probe` leaves no run stretch).
148	    fn letters(&self) -> (char, char) {
149	        (
150	            self.warmup.as_ref().map_or('-', |s| s.letter),
151	            self.during.as_ref().map_or('-', |s| s.letter),
152	        )
153	    }
154	}
155	
156	/// One-line tally of the runs' composite grades, best first:
157	/// `7A 1B 1D 1F`, absent letters omitted.
158	///
159	/// - Printed beside the median because a median is a statement
160	///   about the typical run, and qualification is a question about
161	///   the bad one: a box clean on seven runs of ten reports a
162	///   median of A while three runs saw the machine move. The tally
163	///   cannot hide a tail.

content.text:
The rung's work is done and validated — **please review**. What changed:

**The mechanism** (the interesting part found during implementation): the settle cell was timing-only *because the clock series never escaped `warmup_and_probe`* — only an end-sample summary survived into `RunOutput`, so the report's recomputation had nothing to gate on. The fix scores settle in the harness while the series is alive and carries the verdict as `RunOutput::warm_settle`; the report just prints it.

- `freq.rs` gained `clock_stable` and its 1% tolerance, moved from the harness so the warm exit and the settle scan read one rule from one home.
- `gauge::settle` now takes the clock series and accepts a suffix only when it grades A on timing *and* held its clock; the settled suffix's **median** GHz names the state (one odd read can't), and a box with no readable driver keeps the bare time.
- The cell reads `0.01s @4.09GHz` (style matching the step cell's `@1.90s`), `not settled` and blanks unchanged; the settle column widened 11→15.
- `Settle::At` became a struct variant; qualify's `parse_settle` learned the new form in the same commit, and its read-but-not-scored quarantine is untouched (test still enforces it).
- New test `settle_waits_for_the_clock`: flat timing under a climbing clock must wait for the clock to hold and name the state — the 3900x powersave defect in miniature. 80 tests pass, clippy clean, installed as 0.26.0-1.

**Seen live, first run on this box**: warmup row `0.01s @4.09GHz`, bench row stepping at 1.90s — the cell now says warmup certified a *boosted* state and the bench watched the box leave it. When a powersave run parks at base, the cell will say `@3.79GHz` and the mystery of "settled instantly, then F" reads directly off the report.

One honest limit, unchanged from the spec: when the box genuinely holds one state through warmup and transitions only mid-bench, no warmup-scoped cell can predict it — the naming is what turns that case diagnosable.

The rung is flipped `(done)` with its as-built delta in Ladder details. Say the word and I'll write the description and show it for the push review.

It surprised me for a second too, but the state column explains it completely — and the gap-5 series is actually the *least* mysterious data this box has ever produced:

**Gap 5: the idle resets the box, so every run replays the same trajectory.** Five idle seconds drop the chip out of boost. Each child then starts from the same cold state, and under load the chip snaps to 4.09 GHz within the first probe interval — that's why settle reads exactly 0.01s (one probe gap, the cell's resolution: "flat from the first probe"). Warmup, capped at 1.5s, certifies 4.09 GHz honestly — the box really is settled there. But sustained load on this box takes ~2+ seconds to provoke the climb into the ~4.53 GHz top state (your 2026-08-02 finding: sustained load climbs, bursts hold the slow state), so the climb lands *inside the 5s bench window* every single time: five runs, five mid-bench transitions, 1D 4F. Perfectly reproducible because the 5s idle makes the starting state deterministic.

**Gap 0: each run inherits the previous run's state, so everything varies.** Back-to-back, some children start already in the 4.5x state (runs 5-9: settled @4.52-4.54, means 21.8-22.0, mostly A — the box was already at the top and *stayed* there), some start at 4.09 and either hold it (run 1, A at 24.2 ns) or straddle the climb (runs 2-4, 10: D/C/F). The settle-time scatter is just where in the inherited trajectory each run happened to begin.

Two things worth savoring: your means now pair with named states — ~21.9 ns is the 4.53 GHz state, ~22-24 ns the 4.09 GHz state — and this *directly measures* the states the block's "Seam-clock attribution" entry could only infer from timing ratios (it guessed ~3.79/4.17/4.35; under today's policy the real ladder reads 4.09 and ~4.53). And it's the sharpest evidence yet for your earlier X/Y point: the gap between runs doesn't just add noise, it selects which experiment you're running.

One design implication to keep in mind, not act on now: the 1.5s warm cap can never absorb a transition that needs ~2s of sustained load to trigger, so on this box "settled" will systematically mean "settled in the entry state" for cold starts. That's the dynamic-warmup / suggest-freq territory, and the pin-at-base-clock default kills the whole problem by removing the climb.

The plain version: with a 5-second rest, the computer always starts its speed-up sequence from the same place, and the jump to top speed happens a couple of seconds in — right in the middle of measurement, every time. With no rest, each run starts wherever the last one left the machine, so results wander. The new speed labels in the table are what let us read this off directly instead of guessing.

content.text:
The experiment confirms the mechanism — and adds a twist:

```
  run   warmup  bench    worst   settle           mean
  1     A       A        A       1.77s @4.52GHz   22.0 ns
  2     A       B        B       2.94s @4.51GHz   22.5 ns
  3     B       D        D       not              23.6 ns
  4     A       F        F       1.78s @4.50GHz   22.4 ns
  5     A       F        F       2.61s @4.52GHz   23.6 ns
```

**Confirmed**: with `--settle-time 3`, the climb moved inside warmup exactly as predicted — settle now reads 1.77-2.94s **@4.50-4.52 GHz**, warmup certifies the *top* state instead of the 4.09 entry state, and run 3 honestly reports "not settled" instead of a fake instant. Your rule — stay in warmup until it settles or the budget runs out — is what the code does, and with a budget that covers the climb it reaches the state you actually wanted certified. The defect in the defaults was quantitative, not structural: ~1.55s of sustained warm load against a ~2s climb.

**The twist**: the grades still didn't all flip to A (1A 1B 1D 2F) — even after certifying the top state, three runs watched the box *leave* it mid-bench. One honest caveat before reading too much into that: **I'm running on this box right now** — this session's own load and heat are in those numbers, and your earlier clean-box runs are the trustworthy baseline. But the pattern (run 1 clean, degradation growing through the series) smells like thermal: we think consecutive top-state dwells heat the package and boost starts retreating. Either way the conclusion is the same one this cycle is already built on: this box's top state isn't reliably sustainable, and the base-clock pin — which removes both the climb and the retreat — remains the real fix, with the seam-clock samples (now in the record rung's spec) as the proof it held.

The spec edits you asked for are in: the record rung carries seam-sampled clock (per-block/per-run min/max/median frequency, pin self-verification, the hid-the-climb rationale), and the Seam-clock Todo keeps only the report-labeling half, its inferred states note upgraded to the measured 4.09/4.53.

Worth considering when you're back at a quiet box: rerun this `--settle-time 3` experiment without me running — if the grades clean up, the residual instability was partly me; if not, it's the box's thermal envelope. The plain version: warming up longer does fix the "certified the wrong speed" problem — three seconds is enough, the option already exists — but this machine still won't hold its top speed through a run, so locking the speed down stays the plan that actually makes runs repeatable.

content.text:
Each of your three questions has a crisp answer, and your data just falsified part of my earlier story:

**Why the settle variance is wide — the cell measures "when the last disturbance during warmup happened", not a ramp length.** Settle is the start of the earliest stretch that stays flat *through the end of warmup*. So one clock flip at t=4.5s of a 6.5s warm makes the cell read `4.53s` even if the first 4.5s were glass-flat. On a box that hops states at random times, that number inherits the randomness of the *last* hop. That's also why runs 2 and 8 read "not settled" yet benched A/B — their last wobble happened to land inside the final window.

**And your run 1 (gap-5 set) breaks my "~2s of sustained load provokes the climb" story**: `0.01s @4.09GHz` with `--settle-time 5` means the box sat at 4.09 GHz, flat, through *five-plus seconds* of sustained load — then climbed mid-bench anyway. So the climb isn't a fixed-delay ramp; the transition time is stochastic (thermal and history dependent, we think). Which answers "can the 3900x settle at all": under this policy, **it doesn't settle — it dwells**. It holds a state for seconds at a time (run 4 held ~10s across warm and bench and graded A), but the residency times are random with heavy tails. "Settle" assumes convergence to a final state; this box is a two-state system with no final state. That is the cleanest justification yet for the pin: you can't wait out a coin that keeps flipping.

**On `--min-settle-time`: it already exists — it's `--settle-time` itself.** The process warm runs the full `--settle-time` unconditionally; the adaptive stretch after it is the only part that exits early. So in every run you just posted, warmup was ≥5s regardless of what the settle cell said. The `0.01s` never meant "warmed for 10ms" — it means "flat from 10ms through the end of the full warm", which with settle-time 5 is actually the *strongest* flatness claim in the table. The header's `warm=used/budget` shows the real duration. No new flag needed; what might be needed is the cell not inviting that misreading (printing `0.01s/5.1s` is one option — happy to consider it).

**Block rates: yes.** Blocks are exactly measurement windows (sleep-separated groups of ~50ms batches), every batch boundary is a seam, and the seam sampling we just put in the record rung's spec reads the clock at each one — so beginning/end-of-block rates, and min/max/median per block and per run, all fall out of the same samples. Nothing extra to design.

The plain version: the settle number on your machine mostly records when the last speed-flip happened during warmup, which is random — because your machine never truly finishes warming up; it just lingers at one speed or the other for unpredictable stretches. The warmup minimum you asked for already exists as `--settle-time`. And yes: once we record the clock at every measurement boundary, you'll have the per-block speed readings you want, which is already in the plan.

These findings (stochastic transitions, dwell-not-settle, the 5s-flat-then-climb run) are prime evidence for the cycle records — want me to fold them into the block's pinning-experiment subsection before we push this rung?

message.content:
It's late one, but one more Q: In your opinion is custom.md or custom-family.md needed or is the information in there suitable
to be included in agent-files?

content.text:
My opinion: the *layer* is structurally necessary, but the two files serve different purposes and deserve different verdicts.

**custom.md: needed, and cheap.** Its job is to be the universally-named socket. Pinned files must stay byte-identical across every member, so when prose.md or the checklists say "the commands are in custom.md", they need one stable name that exists in every project — member or not. Without it, pinned text would have to name a per-project file, which breaks pinning itself. Eleven lines buys that indirection; I'd keep it forever.

**custom-family.md: needed today, but overweight, and its content decomposes into four pieces with four different fates:**

- **Medium and validation** — irreducibly project-specific ("the artifact is the iiac-perf CLI", `cargo test --bins` as fast validation, the version promise). This *cannot* be pinned: a pinned file may carry medium conditionals (versioning.md does), but the choice of validation commands is a project decision, not derivable from "it's Rust". This is the layer's permanent resident.
- **Membership** (member name, template path) — data, not instruction, and the file already says so itself: it belongs in `.vc-config.toml` and sits here only because `vc-x1 config --validate` rejects unknown keys. Leaves when the tool learns the keys.
- **Messaging** — the interesting case. It's ~90% family-generic; the only member-specific atom is the mailbox filename, which is just `<member-name>.md`. Once membership lives in config, the pinned files *could* carry messaging parameterized by that value. But the family already decided this the other way on 2026-08-07 — member-only text in pinned files is dead text for non-members — and that argument survives the parameterization. So messaging stays in the layer unless the family accepts member-conditioned pinned text the way it accepts medium-conditioned text. I could argue either side; I lean toward respecting the 2026-08-07 call.
- **The dogfood log** — a per-member *record*, not a rule, and records live in `notes/`. It sits in the layer for adjacency to the rules it critiques, but nothing breaks if it moves to `notes/dogfood.md` with a pointer. This is the easiest slimming available.

So the endgame I'd sketch: custom.md stays as the socket, membership migrates to config, the dogfood log migrates to notes, and custom-family.md shrinks to medium/validation plus messaging — at which point the custom/custom-family *split* (whose whole purpose is keeping custom.md's family-wide diff at one line) is worth re-examining, since a two-section file may no longer justify two files. None of this is urgent, and all of it is convergence material rather than something to change unilaterally — if you want, next session I can distill this into a dogfood entry or a backlog item so it reaches the family's review rather than living in tonight's transcript.

The plain version: keep the tiny pointer file — it's the fixed address every shared rule can reference. The family file is doing four jobs, and only one of them (this project's build-and-test commands) truly has to live there; the rest could migrate to the config file, the notes, and possibly the shared rules, shrinking it toward nothing over time.

message.content: Actaully I didn't mean remove I meant the "policy" information you currently have in the custom* files should/could be moved into non-custom agent-files. There certainly information that need to be in custom*, account names, column widths but there should be specified. Thoughts?

content.text:
Agreed — and that's a sharper principle than my remove/keep framing: **policy in pinned files, parameters in custom***. The test for any line in custom* would be: if two members diffed this text, would a difference be a *disagreement* (then it's policy, and belongs pinned where the diff becomes a reviewable proposal) or just an *identity* (then it's a parameter: a name, a path, a command string, a width)? Custom* should hold only the second kind.

Measured against that, the current files are partly there already:

- **Validation is the model citizen** — this split already exists. The pinned checklists define the two slots (full validation at per-commit step 5, fast at ladder step 3) and AGENTS.md owns the exit-status rule; custom-family fills the slots with this project's command strings. Rule pinned, values custom. Nothing to move but the framing prose.
- **Messaging is the main violator.** Mark-never-delete, thin pointers, check-at-acquaint, push-then-record — all family policy, sitting in the layer since 2026-08-07 because the mailbox path needs a member name. Under your principle it moves pinned, *parameterized*: "at acquaint, a member checks `<messages-repo>/<member>.md`", with the repo path and member name as declared values. And that dissolves the 2026-08-07 dead-text objection cleanly: a pinned rule conditioned on a declared parameter is simply inert where the parameter is absent — exactly how versioning.md's "if Rust / if Python" conditionals already work. Non-members carry the rule but it binds to nothing.
- **Membership** is already pure parameters, just parked in the wrong file until `vc-x1 config` learns the keys.
- **The dogfood log** is neither policy nor parameter — it's a per-member *record*, so it stays out of pinned no matter what (notes/ being its natural long-term home).

Worth naming: this is the same schema/instance split vc-x1 built for its config — `vc-config.md` is pinned policy-plus-schema, `.vc-config.md` is instance values — so the family already believes in this shape for tooling; you're proposing it for the instruction set itself. It would want one new pinned convention stated once ("a pinned rule may reference a parameter declared in the project layer; an undeclared parameter makes the rule inert") and then the messaging section migrates under it.

This is squarely convergence work: a dedicated convention cycle, proposed the usual way (edit our pinned copies, the diff is the proposal), and it deserves vc-x1's eyes since it reverses a rule they took from us. It's late — want me to capture this as a backlog entry (or a dogfood-log stub) so tonight's reasoning survives to that cycle, and leave the actual migration for when it's picked up?

message.content: yes, capture it as a backlog entry and we'll review it tomorrow and then express our opinion with vc-x1.
